section_summary: This section continues a broad history of the Japanese press, tracing its development from Meiji-era regulation and party journalism through commercialization, mass circulation, technological change, news-agency consolidation, and wartime propaganda and controls. It discusses the rise and decline of major newspapers, the formation of the Domei News Agency, and the transformation of correspondents and publishers under war conditions. Pages 95–96 begin Hideo Ono’s separate study of the postwar press, reviewing wartime newspaper mergers and introducing the Occupation authorities’ press reforms, limited censorship, and promotion of professional ethics.

subfiles.title: History of the Japanese Press (continuation)
subfiles.about: A historical survey of Japanese newspapers and news agencies from early Meiji regulation through commercialization, mass journalism, and wartime control.
subfiles.summary: The continuation begins with Meiji newspaper and libel laws, political-party journalism, and the evolution from elite and popular papers into national mass-circulation dailies. It follows the growth of the Asahi, Mainichi, Yomiuri, Jiji Shimpo, and other papers through war reporting, new printing and communications technologies, advertising, labor disputes, and competition with radio. Later pages describe the decline or absorption of older papers, the formation of Rengo and Domei, and the increasing use of the press for state propaganda. By the China and Pacific wars, correspondents, mechanized reporting systems, and a centralized national news agency had become integral to the war effort.

subfiles.title: The Post-War Press in Japan
subfiles.from: Hideo Ono, Director of the Journalism Research Institute, Tokyo University
subfiles.about: An account of the wartime consolidation of Japanese newspapers and the initial press reforms imposed after Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: Ono explains how Japan merged news agencies and papers, rationed newsprint and set one paper per prefecture; air raids devastated production; after surrender GHQ abolished controls, dissolved Domei and encouraged an independent press under limited censorship stressing factual reporting, ethics and journalism education.
